# Garbage Collection

Objects that are not used are collected by the garbage collector. This process
allows the application to dispose from the objects that are not needed anymore
and makes room for new objects that are yet to be created. While we should not
worry much about this process, it is good to keep an eye on it as we may be
creating too many unnecessary objects, as shown in this example.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [Codex CLI](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11096431-openai-codex-cli-getting-started)

- [JDK Mission Control (JMC)](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/products-jmc9-downloads.html)

2. Specify the version of Java

   Please note that this file will contain other information, which is excluded

## Build the application

The following examples require the application to be built.

```shell
./mvnw clean package
```

(*Optional*) Verify that the JAR file was created

```shell
tree --sort=name './target/libs'
```

There should be one JAR file

```
./target/libs
└── garbage-collection-1.0.0.jar

1 directory, 1 file
```

Some of the following commands dump JFR files into a `jfr` directory. Make sure
that the `jfr` directory exists.

```shell
rm -rf './jfr'
mkdir -p './jfr'
```

## Create custom configuration

This example will analyse garbage collection. The TLAB (Thread Local Allocation
Buffer) data is not collected by either the *default* nor the *profile*
configurations. This provides insight on how memory is being used by the
application, such as what objects are being created and from where. Create a new
configuration that captures the TLAB’s events.

1. Create the custom configuration

   ```shell
   jfr configure \
     jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB#enabled=true \
     jdk.ObjectAllocationOutsideTLAB#enabled=true \
     jdk.PromoteObjectInNewPLAB#enabled=true \
     jdk.PromoteObjectOutsidePLAB#enabled=true \
     --output './jfr/custom.jfc'
   ```

   Alternatively, use the interactive option, as shown below, and follow the
   provided instructions.

   ```shell
   jfr configure --interactive --output './jfr/custom.jfc'
   ```

   Select option `4`, to collect the TLAB data, and accept the default for the
   rest.

   ```
   ============== .jfc Configuration Wizard ============
   This wizard will generate a JFR configuration file by
   asking 12 questions. Press ENTER to use the default
   value, or type Q to abort the wizard.

   Garbage Collector: Normal (default)
   1. Off
   2. Normal
   3. Detailed
   4. High, incl. TLABs/PLABs (may cause many events)
   5. All, incl. Heap Statistics (may cause long GCs)
   4
   Using: High, incl. TLABs/PLABs (may cause many events)
   ...
   ```

2. (*Optional*) A `.jfc` file will be created. This file can be saved anywhere
   on the filesystem as long as it is accessible. For this example, the `.jfc`
   is saved under the `jfr` directory.

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './jfr'
   ```

   The custom configuration

   ```
   ./jfr
   └── custom.jfc

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

   The `.jfr` file is an XML file and can be viewed and edited manually.

## Identify overuse of garbage collection

1. Run the application and start flight recorder with the custom configuration
   (`./jfr/custom.jfc`)

   ```shell
   java \
     -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=30s,delay=5s,name='GC',filename='./jfr/demo-before-fix.jfr',settings='./jfr/custom.jfc' \
     -jar './target/libs/garbage-collection-1.0.0.jar'
   ```

   The application will terminate automatically after 40 seconds.

   (*Optional*) Verify that the JFR file was created.

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './jfr'
   ```

   The recording

   ```
   ./jfr
   ├── custom.jfc
   └── demo-before-fix.jfr

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

2. Open the recording file (`./jfr/demo-before-fix.jfr`), in JDK Mission Control

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/jfr/demo-before-fix.jfr"
   ```

   The memory pane provides a more accurate view of which objects are causing
   this problem.

   ![Memory](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20Memory%20-%20Before%20Fix.png)

   We can obtain similar information from the TLAB allocations pane.

   ![TLAB Allocations](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20TLAB%20Allocation%20-%20Before%20Fix.png)

   Note that the stack trace also shows where these objects are being created.

3. Analyse the recording file (`./jfr/demo-before-fix.jfr`) with a custom
   program

   A Java program can open a JFR recording file, analyse each event, and
   identify the methods responsible for the highest object allocation. The
   example below reads the recording file, filters for
   `jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB` and `jdk.ObjectAllocationOutsideTLAB` events,
   and counts the frequency of each method along with the total allocated
   memory. Methods with higher frequencies are likely contributing to excessive
   object allocation.

   ```java
   #!/usr/bin/env -S java --source 25

   import module java.base;
   import module jdk.jfr;

   public static void main(final String[] args) {
       if (args.length < 1 || args.length > 2) {
           System.err.println("Usage: ./tools/PrintObjectAllocation <RECORDING-FILE> [<METHOD-REGEX>]");
           System.exit(1);
       }

       final Path path = Path.of(args[0]);
       final Predicate<String> predicate = createPredicateFromArgs(args);
       final Map<String, AllocationStats> results = compute(path, predicate);

       System.out.printf("%-60s %15s %10s%n", "Method", "Total bytes", "Count");
       results.entrySet()
               .stream()
               .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, AllocationStats>comparingByValue().reversed())
               .limit(20)
               .forEach(entry -> {
                   final String method = truncate(entry.getKey(), 60);
                   final AllocationStats stats = entry.getValue();
                   System.out.printf("%-60s %15d %10d%n", method, stats.totalBytes, stats.count);
               });
   }

   private static Map<String, AllocationStats> compute(final Path path, final Predicate<String> predicate) {
       final Map<String, AllocationStats> results = new HashMap<>();

       final Set<String> eventsOfInterest = Set.of("jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB", "jdk.ObjectAllocationOutsideTLAB");

       try (RecordingFile recordingFile = new RecordingFile(path)) {
           while (recordingFile.hasMoreEvents()) {
               final RecordedEvent event = recordingFile.readEvent();

               if (eventsOfInterest.contains(event.getEventType().getName())) {
                   final RecordedStackTrace stackTrace = event.getStackTrace();
                   final String method = formatStack(stackTrace, predicate);
                   final long size = event.getLong("allocationSize");

                   results.merge(method, AllocationStats.of(size), AllocationStats::add);
               }
           }

           return results;
       } catch (final IOException e) {
           throw new UncheckedIOException("Failed to read recording file " + path, e);
       }
   }

   private static String formatStack(final RecordedStackTrace stackTrace, final Predicate<String> classOfInterest) {
       if (stackTrace == null || stackTrace.getFrames().isEmpty()) {
           return "Unknown (stack trace is not available)";
       }

       return formatStack(stackTrace.getFrames(), classOfInterest);
   }

   private static String formatStack(final List<RecordedFrame> frames, final Predicate<String> classOfInterest) {
       for (final RecordedFrame frame : frames) {
           final String className = frame.getMethod().getType().getName();
           if (classOfInterest.test(className)) {
               return formatFrame(frame);
           }
       }

       /* Fallback if no application frame found */
       return formatFrame(frames.getFirst());
   }

   private static String formatFrame(final RecordedFrame frame) {
       final RecordedMethod method = frame.getMethod();
       return method.getType().getName() + "." + method.getName() + ":" + frame.getLineNumber();
   }

   private static Predicate<String> createPredicateFromArgs(final String[] args) {
       return args.length == 2
               ? Pattern.compile(args[1]).asMatchPredicate()
               : t -> !(t.startsWith("java.")
               || t.startsWith("javax.")
               || t.startsWith("sun.")
               || t.startsWith("jdk.")
               || t.startsWith("com.sun."));
   }

   private record AllocationStats(long totalBytes, long count) implements Comparable<AllocationStats> {

       private static final Comparator<AllocationStats> NATURAL_ORDER =
               Comparator.comparingLong(AllocationStats::totalBytes)
                       .thenComparing(AllocationStats::count);

       public static AllocationStats of(final long totalBytes) {
           return new AllocationStats(totalBytes, 1);
       }

       public AllocationStats add(final AllocationStats other) {
           return new AllocationStats(totalBytes + other.totalBytes, count + other.count);
       }

       @Override
       public int compareTo(final AllocationStats other) {
           return NATURAL_ORDER.compare(this, other);
       }
   }

   public static String truncate(final String original, final int maxLength) {
       if (maxLength <= original.length()) {
           return "..." + original.substring(original.length() - maxLength + 3);
       }

       return original;
   }
   ```

   We are interested in identifying where in our code objects are being created,
   even if the allocation occurs in a downstream method. For example, while
   `Integer.valueOf()` creates the object, this offers limited insight. In such
   cases, we walk the stack until we find a class of interest—specifically, one
   within the `demo` package.

   ```shell
   ./tools/PrintObjectAllocation './jfr/demo-before-fix.jfr' 'demo\..*'
   ```

   The program will display methods from where most objects are created.

   ```
   Method                                                           Total bytes      Count
   demo.Worker.run:18                                                    488016      30501
   java.util.ArrayList.iterator:1030                                        928         29
   demo.Worker.run:17                                                        96          3
   Unknown (stack trace is not available)                                    72          3
   ...lang.classfile.instruction.ConstantInstruction.ofLoad:234              24          1
   jdk.jfr.internal.PlatformRecording$2.run:689                              24          1
   jdk.jfr.internal.periodic.PeriodicEvents.doPeriodic:120                   24          1
   ```

4. Ask Codex to investigate the recording without telling it where the problem
   is.

   The previous JMC view already points us toward memory allocation. In a real
   investigation, we may not know that yet. In that case, let Codex inspect the
   recording with JDK tools and ask it to identify which event families deserve
   closer inspection.

   This is less deterministic than a focused extraction, because the agent has
   to choose how to inspect the recording. It is useful as a discovery step, but
   its conclusions still need to be backed by JFR-derived evidence.

   ```shell
   rm -rf 'target/jfr-exploration'
   mkdir -p 'target/jfr-exploration'
   cp './jfr/demo-before-fix.jfr' 'target/jfr-exploration/demo-before-fix.jfr'

   codex exec \
     --ephemeral \
     --cd "${PWD}/target/jfr-exploration" \
     --add-dir "${PWD}/src/main/java" \
     --sandbox read-only \
     --model gpt-6.1-terra \
     --config 'model_reasoning_effort="medium"' \
     --skip-git-repo-check \
     --output-last-message "${PWD}/target/jfr-exploration/gc-ai-investigation.md" \
     - <<'EOF' > 'target/jfr-exploration/gc-ai-investigation-run.log' 2>&1
   You are investigating an unknown Java performance issue from a JFR recording.

   Use `demo-before-fix.jfr` as the runtime evidence. Use JDK command-line tools,
   such as `jfr summary` and focused `jfr print` commands, to inspect the
   recording. Use the added source directory only to connect suspicious runtime
   evidence to application code.

   Do not assume the issue is allocation, garbage collection, CPU, lock
   contention, I/O, exceptions, or anything else until the recording supports it.
   Do not modify files.

   Investigate:
   1. which event categories or event types look dominant or abnormal
   2. whether the evidence points to allocation/GC, CPU, lock contention, I/O,
      exceptions, or another issue
   3. which application source lines are most likely involved
   4. what focused JFR extraction should be run next to confirm the hypothesis
   5. what a developer should inspect in JDK Mission Control

   Do not use Markdown links or absolute file paths. When citing source evidence,
   use paths relative to src/main/java, such as demo/Worker.java:18.

   Return a concise investigation report with the commands used and the evidence
   that supports each conclusion. Keep the report under 60 lines.
   EOF
   ```

   Codex explores the recording and identifies where to investigate next.

   ~~~markdown
   The strongest hypothesis is sustained allocation and CPU work in the worker’s map scan. Frequent young GCs accompany it, but recorded GC pauses account for only about 95 ms of the 30-second recording.

   - **Dominant events:** `jfr summary` reports 48,432 parallel GC phase events, 30,331 new-TLAB allocation events, 4,457 allocation samples, and 208 young GCs. Parallel phase counts include work by GC threads; they are not 48,432 separate collections.
   - **Allocation:** 4,444 of 4,457 allocation samples are `Integer` objects with a stack through `Integer.valueOf` and `demo/Worker.java:18`. Samples represent estimated allocation activity, not individual object counts.
   - **CPU:** 1,417 of 1,418 execution samples are on `pool-1-thread-1`; 814 include `demo/Worker.java:18` and 602 include line 17. These are sampled runnable stacks, not exact CPU-time measurements.
   - **GC:** All 208 collections are young G1 collections. Their recorded pauses total approximately 95.3 ms; the longest is 0.666 ms. Allocation pressure is clear, but long GC pauses are not supported by this recording.
   - **Other causes:** No monitor-enter, file or socket I/O, or exception-throw events were recorded. That does not rule them out: event enablement and thresholds limit what JFR captures.

   The relevant code repeatedly scans 10,000 map values in `demo/Worker.java:15`–`18`. The primitive `id` in `demo/MapValue.java:3` is boxed for the `Map<Integer, ...>` lookup at line 18, consistent with the allocation stacks. Inspect whether this repeated lookup and scan are necessary.

   Commands used:

   ```text
   jfr summary demo-before-fix.jfr
   jfr print --events jdk.ObjectAllocationSample --stack-depth 12 demo-before-fix.jfr
   jfr print --events jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB --stack-depth 8 demo-before-fix.jfr
   jfr print --events jdk.ExecutionSample --stack-depth 12 demo-before-fix.jfr
   jfr print --events jdk.GarbageCollection,jdk.CPULoad,jdk.ExceptionStatistics demo-before-fix.jfr
   ```

   The printed events were also counted with `awk`. Next, extract allocation samples and new-TLAB events together with execution samples over the full recording, grouping by class, thread and stack; compare their timeline with `jdk.GarbageCollection` and `jdk.GCHeapSummary`. This tests whether the same lookup remains responsible throughout and whether heap use repeatedly falls after young GC.

   In JDK Mission Control, inspect the allocation views by class and stack, the worker thread’s execution-sample flame graph, and the GC timeline and heap before/after collections. Correlate their timestamps and check recording settings before drawing conclusions from absent events.
   ~~~

## Fix the high garbage collection issue

Our program is converting primitive `int` to the wrapper `Integer` object
through autoboxing, introduce back in Java 1.5, far too many times, enough to
make an impact on the garbage collector. Autoboxing is not a bad thing and do
not try to optimise prematurely.

We can mitigate this problem by changing the type to the most commonly needed
type, `Integer`, to avoid autoboxing.

1. Update the type of the `id` field in the `MapValue` class

   Copy the updated code from the `fixtures/01-avoid-autoboxing/` directory.

   ```shell
   rsync --archive 'fixtures/01-avoid-autoboxing/' .
   ```

   The [`MapValue` class](./src/main/java/demo/MapValue.java) should look like
   the following example.

   ```java
   package demo;

   public record MapValue(Integer id) {}
   ```

2. Rebuild the project

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

3. Rerun the application and collect the flight recording data to verify whether
   this solution addressed the problem or not.

   ```shell
   java \
     -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=30s,delay=5s,name='GC',filename='./jfr/demo-after-fix.jfr',settings='./jfr/custom.jfc' \
     -jar './target/libs/garbage-collection-1.0.0.jar'
   ```

4. Verify that the garbage collection problem is now resolved using JMC
   (`./jfr/demo-after-fix.jfr`)

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/jfr/demo-after-fix.jfr"
   ```

   ![Memory](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20Memory%20-%20After%20Fix.png)

   ![TLAB Allocations](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20TLAB%20Allocation%20-%20After%20Fix.png)

5. Contrast the recording files with a custom program

   ```shell
   './tools/PrintObjectAllocation' './jfr/demo-before-fix.jfr' 'demo\..*'
   ```

   The program will display methods from where most objects are created.

   ```
   Method                                                           Total bytes      Count
   demo.Worker.run:18                                                    488016      30501
   java.util.ArrayList.iterator:1030                                        928         29
   demo.Worker.run:17                                                        96          3
   Unknown (stack trace is not available)                                    72          3
   ...lang.classfile.instruction.ConstantInstruction.ofLoad:234              24          1
   jdk.jfr.internal.PlatformRecording$2.run:689                              24          1
   jdk.jfr.internal.periodic.PeriodicEvents.doPeriodic:120                   24          1
   ```

   Let us now compare the sample counts from the second recording, taken after
   the fix was applied.

   ```shell
   './tools/PrintObjectAllocation' './jfr/demo-after-fix.jfr' 'demo\..*'
   ```

   The program will display methods from where most objects are created.

   ```
   Method                                                           Total bytes      Count
   jdk.internal.classfile.impl.EntryMap.<init>:77                         16400          1
   demo.Worker.run:17                                                       640         20
   jdk.internal.classfile.impl.SplitConstantPool.utf8Entry:487               64          1
   ```

   The large number of allocations seen in the initial recording is no longer
   present, indicating that our refactoring was successful.

6. Contrast the recording files with codex

   We can also ask Codex to compare the before-fix and after-fix allocation
   summaries. This keeps the model grounded in the JFR-derived evidence rather
   than asking it to infer whether the change helped.

   ```shell
   rm -rf 'target/jfr-ai'
   mkdir -p 'target/jfr-ai'

   './tools/PrintObjectAllocation' \
     './jfr/demo-before-fix.jfr' \
     'demo\..*' > 'target/jfr-ai/allocations-before.txt'

   './tools/PrintObjectAllocation' \
     './jfr/demo-after-fix.jfr' \
     'demo\..*' > 'target/jfr-ai/allocations-after.txt'

   codex exec \
     --ephemeral \
     --cd "${PWD}/target/jfr-ai" \
     --sandbox read-only \
     --model gpt-6.1-terra \
     --config 'model_reasoning_effort="medium"' \
     --skip-git-repo-check \
     --output-last-message "${PWD}/target/jfr-ai/gc-ai-verification.md" \
     - <<'EOF' > 'target/jfr-ai/gc-ai-verification-run.log' 2>&1
   Compare `allocations-before.txt` and `allocations-after.txt`.

   Use only these two JFR-derived summaries. Explain whether the allocation
   hotspot was reduced, which evidence supports that conclusion, and what
   residual allocations remain. Keep the answer concise.
   EOF
   ```

   Codex compares the before-fix and after-fix allocation evidence.

   ```markdown
   Yes. The dominant reported allocation site, `demo.Worker.run:18`, fell from **488,016 bytes across 30,501 allocations** to no entry in the after summary.

   The after summary still reports **640 bytes across 20 allocations** at `demo.Worker.run:17`, plus **16,464 bytes across two JDK class-file allocation sites**. The summaries show reported allocations, but do not establish that the original site was completely eliminated or that the recordings covered equivalent workloads.
   ```
